title: Complete Legal Aid
description: Bilingual legal-aid platform connecting Bangladeshi citizens with verified lawyers — escrow payments, encrypted evidence, and four AI agents on one real-time stack.
impact: Produced a deployable justice platform rather than a demo: Docker Compose brings up PostgreSQL, Redis, Daphne, nginx, and certbot with automatic TLS, and production settings actively refuse to start with DEBUG on, SQLite, or default passwords.
overview: Legal help in Bangladesh is hard to price, hard to verify, and hard to reach. CLA puts citizens, verified lawyers, and administrators on one platform in both Bangla and English, and treats the awkward parts of the problem — proving a lawyer is real, holding money safely until work is done, and keeping evidence private — as first-class features rather than afterthoughts.
problem: A citizen looking for legal help has no reliable way to check that a lawyer is genuine, no protection when paying up front, and no safe channel for sensitive documents. Lawyers, meanwhile, lose hours drafting standard filings by hand. Both sides fall back on personal referrals, which excludes anyone without the right contacts.
solution: Every role gets its own dashboard over a shared Django backend. Payments run through an escrow flow with an immutable ledger, so money is only released against completed work and the books can be proven consistent. Evidence never sits at a public URL — nginx denies /media by default and files are reachable only through short-lived signed links. Four server-side AI agents handle triage, case-strength estimation, drafting, and emergency routing, each restricted to an allow-listed set of tools and scoped to the caller's role.
architecture: The stack is event-driven rather than poll-driven: a service or signal pushes through a Redis channel layer into Django Channels, and the browser's WebSocket provider updates the UI directly. Polling exists only as a fallback. The AI layer is deliberately isolated — all keys stay server-side, and every AI feature degrades gracefully to a non-AI path when a key or an optional ML dependency is missing, so a missing API key never takes the platform down.

features.title: Four scoped AI agents
features.description: Counsel Match triages a citizen's problem into a ranked lawyer shortlist; Justice Lens gives a calibrated case-strength estimate with cited articles; Document Forge drafts from a lawyer's own cases and flags unfilled placeholders; Sentinel handles emergency triage with anonymity-respecting NGO routing. All use function-calling against allow-listed tools, stream over SSE, and are throttled per user.

features.title: Escrow payments on an immutable ledger
features.description: SSLCommerz payments flow through a single audited path that writes append-only WalletLedgerEntry records. A reconcile_wallets management command proves the ledger and balances agree.

features.title: Signed-link evidence vault
features.description: Evidence, identity papers, and chat attachments are never served from public URLs. nginx default-denies /media except explicit public folders; everything else is reachable only via short-lived signed links, behind extension, MIME, and magic-byte validation with a 25 MB cap.

features.title: Constitution RAG in plain Bangla
features.description: A Gemini-backed assistant answers in everyday Bangla, retrieving over the Constitution with FAISS so answers cite real articles instead of paraphrasing from memory.

features.title: Ban-aware JWT sessions
features.description: One-hour access tokens with seven-day rotating refresh and a blacklist. Banning a user invalidates their existing tokens immediately rather than waiting for expiry.

features.title: Court-ready bilingual drafting
features.description: Generates bail applications, deeds, notices, and affidavits in Bangla or English from lawyer-owned, database-backed templates that can be shared across the firm.

challenges.challenge: Keeping money movement auditable when payments, refunds, and withdrawals all touch the same balance.
challenges.learned: Routed every balance change through one service instead of letting views update wallets directly, and made the ledger append-only so a mistake produces a correcting entry rather than a silent edit. That made a reconciliation command possible — consistency became something to verify on demand rather than assume.

challenges.challenge: Confidential uploads are easy to leak, because the obvious setup serves them from a guessable static path.
challenges.learned: Inverted the default: nginx denies everything under /media unless explicitly allowed, and private files are reachable only through expiring signed links. Deny-by-default means a new upload type is private until someone deliberately publishes it — the opposite of the usual failure mode.

challenges.challenge: The on-box ML extras (FAISS, sentence-transformers) pull in torch at roughly 2.5 GB, which is unacceptable in a CI image.
challenges.learned: Split them into a separate requirements-ml.txt and made every dependent feature detect their absence and fall back. The Docker image and CI skip them entirely, and the same codebase runs in both shapes without branching.

challenges.challenge: Giving LLM agents real capability without giving them free rein over the database.
challenges.learned: Each agent gets an explicit allow-list of tools and inherits the caller's role, so a citizen's agent cannot reach a lawyer's cases. Capability is granted per tool rather than withheld per query, which is far easier to reason about when reviewing what an agent can actually do.

results.description: Counsel Match, Justice Lens, Document Forge, Sentinel — each role-scoped and tool-restricted
Citizen, lawyer, and admin, each with a separate code-split dashboard
Full i18n with Bangla code-split from the main bundle
PostgreSQL 16, Redis 7, Daphne, nginx, and certbot via one Docker Compose deploy

title: SkillEx
description: Peer skill-exchange platform where people trade what they can teach for what they want to learn — matched semantically, with no money involved.
impact: The OOP brief pushed toward structure that earned its keep: one client boundary on the frontend and an interface-per-service split on the backend meant the embedding provider could be swapped for a local fallback without touching a controller.
overview: An Advanced OOP course project taken past the coursework brief. The interesting constraint is that there is no currency: a match is only useful when two people's offers and wants genuinely complement each other, which turns matching into the core engineering problem rather than a feature bolted on later.
problem: Skill learning is gated by cost, while plenty of people hold knowledge worth trading. Keyword matching is not good enough to pair them — someone offering "React" and someone wanting "frontend development" never meet, even though they should.
solution: Skills are embedded through the Gemini Embedding API and matched by semantic similarity, so related phrasings converge. Because a hosted embedding service is a hard dependency for a course project, the backend falls back to local embeddings whenever no API key is present — the feature degrades in quality rather than disappearing.
architecture: A monorepo with clean seams. The frontend is organised as feature-first vertical slices, and all network access funnels through a single ApiClient singleton, so JWT attachment and error shape live in one place. The backend keeps controllers thin and routes work through service interfaces to implementations, with Flyway owning the schema as versioned SQL.

features.title: Semantic skill matching
features.description: Gemini embeddings place offered and wanted skills in the same vector space, so "React" and "frontend development" match on meaning rather than on shared characters.

features.title: Graceful embedding fallback
features.description: With EMBEDDING_PROVIDER set to api but no key present, the backend silently switches to local embeddings instead of failing the request.

features.title: Single API boundary
features.description: An ApiClient singleton wraps fetch, attaches the JWT, and normalises every response into ApiResponse<T> — so success, error, and message handling are identical across features.

features.title: Versioned schema with Flyway
features.description: Migrations run as ordered SQL on startup, so a fresh clone reaches the current schema without anyone running statements by hand.

features.title: Feature-first frontend slices
features.description: Each domain owns its components, services, and types together, so a feature can be read or removed without tracing through shared folders.

challenges.challenge: A hosted embedding API is a single point of failure for the one feature the product is built around.
challenges.learned: Made the provider a configuration choice with an automatic local fallback rather than a hard dependency. Designing the degraded path first meant the feature had a defined behaviour without a key, instead of an exception.

challenges.challenge: Getting a Spring Boot backend and a Vite frontend running together locally involves MySQL, ports, and migration order.
challenges.learned: Automated it — a pre-start script detects and starts MySQL, waits for port 3306, and ensures the database exists before the backend boots. Setup friction is a real cost on a team project; removing it is worth the scripting.

challenges.challenge: Thin controllers are easy to describe and easy to erode once deadlines arrive.
challenges.learned: Keeping the service as an interface with a separate implementation made the boundary structural rather than a convention. It is harder to leak business logic into a controller when doing so means bypassing a type you would have to go around deliberately.

results.description: Gemini embeddings, with an automatic local fallback
React 19 frontend and Spring Boot 3 backend sharing one migration source
Versioned SQL applied automatically on first run

title: ConvoVerse
description: HCI research prototype where introverted learners rehearse conversations with LLM agents before facing the real thing.
impact: Contributes a reusable interaction pattern rather than a product: staged exposure, reversible actions, and non-evaluative feedback, applicable to any system supporting participation.
overview: An academic Human-Computer Interaction project built on a specific claim: many capable students stay quiet not from lack of knowledge but from lack of rehearsal. ConvoVerse gives them a private space to practise, positioning AI as a facilitator that helps someone feel ready to participate — explicitly not as a substitute for talking to people.
problem: Educational platforms optimise for delivering content and assume participation follows. For students who freeze in discussions, the barrier is social readiness, and every existing option asks them to practise in exactly the public setting they are avoiding.
solution: Difficulty is scaffolded in stages instead of thrown at the user. Observer Mode lets them watch agents converse without participating; then one-on-one with a single peer agent; then a small group where a Peer, a Group Member, and a Facilitator compete for turns. Rewind and Retry lets any exchange be restarted with no penalty.
architecture: The same agent roles are recombined per stage rather than rewritten, so escalating difficulty is a matter of how many agents are present and how they interact. Psychological safety is enforced as a design constraint: no scoring, no public exposure, no forced turn — closing feedback is reflective rather than evaluative.

features.title: Observer Mode
features.description: The user watches AI agents hold a conversation with no expectation of input, so the first exposure carries no risk of being addressed.

features.title: Three distinct agent roles
features.description: A Peer converses as an equal, a Group Member competes for speaking turns, and a Facilitator keeps discussion moving — together modelling the dynamics that make group settings hard.

features.title: Rewind and Retry
features.description: Any exchange can be restarted to try a different response, making exploration free and removing the cost of saying the wrong thing.

features.title: Adaptive pacing
features.description: Conversation speed and complexity respond to the user's comfort rather than following a fixed script.

features.title: Non-evaluative reflection
features.description: Sessions close with reflective prompts rather than a score, keeping the experience about confidence instead of performance.

challenges.challenge: An AI conversation partner risks becoming a substitute for human contact — the opposite of the intended outcome.
challenges.learned: Framed every interaction as rehearsal for a real conversation rather than a replacement, and made the staging always point outward toward participation. The framing is the intervention here; the same agents with different framing would produce a different, worse product.

challenges.challenge: Scoring is the obvious way to show progress, and exactly the wrong mechanic for anxious users.
challenges.learned: Dropped scores entirely in favour of reflective prompts. Any evaluative signal reintroduces the judgement the environment exists to remove, so the safety property has to be enforced by leaving features out.

results.description: Peer, Group Member, and Facilitator, recombined per stage
Observe, one-on-one, then small group
Reflective feedback only — a deliberate design constraint

title: Care Companion
description: Raspberry Pi health rover that monitors vitals, dispenses medication on schedule, and raises alerts for gas, fire, or a panic button.
impact: Built entirely from commodity parts — Pi 4, Arduino UNO, DHT11, MQ-2, a pulse sensor, an L298N driver — keeping the whole prototype within a student budget while covering monitoring, reminders, hazard detection, and mobility.
overview: A microprocessor project that ended up a working prototype: a mobile assistant for patients and elderly people living at home, combining continuous vitals monitoring with physical actions — moving to the patient, opening a medicine drawer, sounding an alarm.
problem: Home care depends on someone being present. Missed medication, an unnoticed fever, a gas leak, or a fall can all go undetected for hours, and commercial monitoring systems are priced out of reach for most households.
solution: Split the work across two processors by what each is good at. An Arduino UNO owns the sensors, where tight timing loops matter; the Raspberry Pi 4 handles vision, voice, decisions, and the web layer. They talk over serial, so a slow decision on the Pi never delays a sensor read.
architecture: The dashboard never talks to hardware. Sensor readings land in MySQL and the UI reads from there, with Django Channels pushing updates over WebSocket. Celery and Redis own scheduled medication reminders, so timing survives a page being closed — the browser is a view onto state, not a participant in control.

features.title: Continuous vitals monitoring
features.description: DHT11 for temperature and a Pulse Sensor Amped for heart rate, sampled on the Arduino and streamed to the Pi over serial for threshold checks.

features.title: Automated medication dispensing
features.description: An SG90 servo opens the correct drawer on schedule with a buzzer prompt, driven by Celery so the timing holds independently of the dashboard.

features.title: Hazard detection
features.description: MQ-2 gas and IR flame sensors raise immediate local alarms and push a notification to caregivers, without waiting on a network round trip.

features.title: Autonomous mobility
features.description: TT gear motors through an L298N driver, with Pi Camera v3 person detection and obstacle avoidance so the rover can reach the patient.

features.title: Voice control
features.description: Wake-word commands let a patient summon or direct the rover without reaching a screen or a button.

features.title: Caregiver dashboard
features.description: Live vitals and trend charts over WebSocket, plus a panic-button feed, reading from the database rather than polling hardware.

challenges.challenge: Sensor sampling and computer vision on one processor make each other unreliable — vision work starves the timing-sensitive reads.
challenges.learned: Gave the Arduino sole ownership of sensors and left the Pi to decisions and vision, with serial between them. Splitting by timing requirement rather than by feature is what made both halves predictable.

challenges.challenge: Medication reminders cannot depend on a browser being open, but the obvious implementation puts the timer in the request cycle.
challenges.learned: Moved scheduling into Celery with Redis as the broker, so reminders fire from a worker regardless of who is watching. Anything with real-world consequences belongs outside the request cycle.

challenges.challenge: Emergency alerts that travel through the web stack inherit its latency, which is the wrong trade for a gas leak.
challenges.learned: Made hazards trigger the local buzzer and LEDs directly on the device, then notify over the network as a second step. The safety-critical path should not depend on anything that can be slow or offline.

results.description: Temperature, pulse, gas, and flame, sampled continuously
Arduino UNO for sensing, Raspberry Pi 4 for decisions and vision
Hazards sound on-device before any network call

title: UniShare
description: Real-time campus marketplace and community app — listings, groups, and chat that update live over a single WebSocket connection.
impact: Shipped with a real test setup — Vitest plus React Testing Library — and GitHub Actions deploying the UI, which is the part most student projects skip.
overview: A university community platform where students list items, form groups, and message each other. The design constraint was that everything social should feel immediate: a new message or listing appears without a refresh, and without the app polling in the background.
problem: Campus buying, selling, and group coordination scatter across Facebook groups and messenger threads, where posts are unsearchable and nothing is scoped to the university. Rebuilding that on request-response alone would mean constant polling to feel current.
solution: One Socket.IO connection per client carries chat, notifications, and listing updates, with REST handling ordinary reads and writes. TanStack Query owns the cache, so a socket event invalidates the affected query rather than the UI hand-patching its own state.
architecture: Better-SQLite3 backs the server — synchronous and embedded, which removes connection-pool handling and async plumbing at this scale. Zod validates payloads at runtime on the client, so data crossing the socket boundary is checked rather than trusted to match its TypeScript type.

features.title: Live chat and notifications
features.description: Socket.IO carries messages and notifications over one duplex connection, with rooms scoping broadcasts to the people who should receive them.

features.title: Cache-driven UI updates
features.description: Socket events invalidate TanStack Query keys instead of mutating component state, so the refetch path is the same whether an update arrived by socket or by navigation.

features.title: Runtime-validated payloads
features.description: Zod schemas check incoming data at the boundary, catching shape mismatches that TypeScript types cannot enforce at runtime.

features.title: Tested and continuously deployed
features.description: Vitest with React Testing Library and JSDOM cover the UI, and GitHub Actions handles deployment.

challenges.challenge: Live updates and a client cache disagree easily — the socket says one thing while the cache still holds another.
challenges.learned: Stopped treating socket payloads as state and treated them as invalidation signals instead. Letting the query layer refetch keeps one source of truth; patching the cache directly from an event is where the two views drift apart.

challenges.challenge: Choosing a database for a project that must be trivial to run locally but still relational.
challenges.learned: Better-SQLite3 is synchronous and embedded, so there is no pool, no daemon, and no await on every query. At campus scale the simplicity is worth more than the concurrency a server-based database would add.

results.description: Chat, notifications, and listing updates share one connection
TypeScript throughout, with route-level code splitting
Vitest suite plus GitHub Actions deployment

title: ChefMate
description: Recipe finder that takes whatever is actually in your kitchen, in plain English, and ranks real recipes by how much of each one you can already make.
impact: Turned a text-matching problem into a retrieval one. Every result carries an explicit match score plus the matched and missing ingredient lists, so the ranking is legible instead of being a number the user has to trust.
overview: Most recipe sites work backwards: pick a dish, then go shopping. ChefMate starts from the ingredients already on hand and finds the closest matches, showing what is missing for each so the trade-off is visible before committing to a dish.
problem: Free-text ingredient input breaks naive matching immediately. "Tomatoes", "tomato", and a typo like "tomatos" are three different strings, and regional names diverge further — aubergine and eggplant are the same vegetable. Exact matching fragments the search space and returns nothing useful.
solution: A normalisation stage runs before any matching. spaCy lemmatises each token to its base form, a hand-curated synonym map reconciles regional names, and rapidfuzz corrects remaining typos against the known ingredient vocabulary at an 80% similarity threshold. Only the cleaned tokens reach the retrieval step, so the model never sees the raw mess.
architecture: Cuisine, diet, and meal-type filters are applied to the dataframe first, which shrinks the candidate set before any vectorisation happens. The surviving recipes are transformed by a fitted TF-IDF vectoriser and queried with k-nearest-neighbours; the model, vectoriser, and dataframe are pickled together so a request only pays for lookup, not training.

features.title: Lemmatisation and synonym mapping
features.description: spaCy's en_core_web_sm reduces each ingredient to its lemma, then a curated map folds regional variants together — courgette to zucchini, garbanzo bean to chickpea, scallion to green onion.

features.title: Fuzzy correction against known vocabulary
features.description: rapidfuzz matches a mistyped ingredient to the closest term actually present in the dataset, accepting it only above an 80% similarity score so wrong corrections are rejected rather than guessed.

features.title: Filter-then-retrieve ordering
features.description: Cuisine, diet, and meal-type filters narrow the dataframe before vectorisation, so kNN searches a small relevant set instead of the whole corpus.

features.title: Transparent match scoring
features.description: Each result reports matched ingredients, missing ingredients, and a percentage computed from their overlap, so a low-ranked recipe explains itself.

challenges.challenge: The same ingredient arrives under many spellings, and exact matching treats each as unrelated.
challenges.learned: Normalisation had to be a distinct pipeline stage rather than a helper sprinkled through the matching code. Once every input passed through one funnel — lemma, then synonym, then fuzzy — the retrieval logic got simpler because it could assume clean tokens.

challenges.challenge: Fitting the vectoriser per request made responses slow enough to feel broken.
challenges.learned: Pickled the trained model, the fitted vectoriser, and the recipe dataframe as one artefact loaded at predict time. Keeping them together matters more than it looks: a vectoriser separated from the data it was fitted on produces silently wrong vectors.

results.description: Lemmatisation, synonym mapping, and fuzzy correction before any matching
Similarity floor below which a correction is rejected rather than guessed
Every recipe shows both lists alongside its overlap score

title: Integrated Healthcare Management System
description: Hospital management system covering appointments, prescriptions, ambulance dispatch, and a blood-donor registry across patient, doctor, and admin roles.
impact: Writing it without a framework meant confronting the problems frameworks normally hide: session fixation, output escaping, and role checks that must not be bypassable by navigating straight to a URL. Migration and demo-seed scripts keep the schema reproducible.
overview: Built on plain PHP and MySQL with no framework, which made every piece of plumbing — routing, sessions, access control, escaping — an explicit decision rather than something inherited. It covers the workflows a small hospital actually runs on, including the ones usually left out of student projects: ambulance booking and a blood bank.
problem: Small clinics run on paper and phone calls. Appointments, prescriptions, ambulance requests, and blood-donor contacts each live in a different notebook, so nobody can answer a simple question like which donors match a patient's blood group right now.
solution: One database behind role-separated interfaces. Patients book appointments and ambulances and read their own records; doctors manage schedules, prescriptions, and medical history; admins oversee doctors, ambulances, and reports. The blood bank is a self-contained module with its own donor registry, stock view, and request queue.
architecture: Every page includes a session guard before it emits any output, so authorisation is decided before a query runs rather than after. A shared Security class centralises the primitives — password_hash at cost 12, random_bytes tokens, htmlspecialchars with ENT_QUOTES for output, filter_var for email — so no page invents its own escaping.

features.title: Three role-separated dashboards
features.description: Patient, doctor, and admin each get their own directory of pages and their own permitted actions, checked per request.

features.title: Blood bank module
features.description: Donor registry with add, edit, and delete, searchable by blood group, plus a stock view and a request queue for matching donors to needs.

features.title: Ambulance dispatch
features.description: Patients submit booking requests and track their own; admins manage the fleet and assign vehicles.

features.title: Clinical records
features.description: Appointments, prescriptions, medical history, health logs, and downloadable reports, each scoped to the patient they belong to.

features.title: Reproducible schema
features.description: db_migrate.php and db_seed_demo.php rebuild the database and populate demo data, so a fresh checkout reaches a working state without manual SQL.

challenges.challenge: Without a framework, an unguarded page is a complete authorisation bypass — the URL is the only thing standing between a patient and another patient's records.
challenges.learned: Made the session guard the first include on every page, before any output. Doing the check after rendering has begun is too late to redirect, and that ordering constraint is exactly what a framework's middleware normally enforces for you.

challenges.challenge: Escaping applied ad hoc at each output site gets missed somewhere, and one miss is an XSS hole.
challenges.learned: Centralised it in a Security class with htmlspecialchars(ENT_QUOTES, UTF-8) and recursive array handling, so nested form input is covered by the same call. Consistency matters more than cleverness here — the risk is the site you forget, not the one you write carefully.

challenges.challenge: Six modules touching one schema drift apart quickly when the database is set up by hand.
challenges.learned: Added migration and seed scripts so the schema has a single source of truth in the repository. Being able to reset to a known state turns schema bugs into reproducible ones.

results.description: Appointments, prescriptions, records, ambulance, blood bank, chatbot
Patient, doctor, and admin with separate page trees
password_hash with bcrypt work factor 12, never plaintext or MD5
